title: Gemilut Chasadim: Kindness for Anyone
hook: a daily act of chesed, however small
carry: chesed goes to rich and poor alike
tomorrow: a rabbi is known by two words from a Psalm. which two, and why?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mar Zutra's bedtime sentence: let go of the day's claims before you sleep. Forgive before sleeping. Today, the other side of the ledger: what you put in.

Someone lets you merge on a packed road. A stranger holds the elevator. A coworker remembers how you take your coffee. None of it makes the news, and the day is lighter anyway. In Pirkei Avot, Simon the Righteous says the world stands on three things: on Torah, on the service of God, and on acts of loving-kindness. So which fits in a day? The third needs no book and no building. It fits in a hallway.
screen: `A MERGE, AN ELEVATOR, A COFFEE.` → `THE WORLD STANDS ON THREE THINGS.` → `THE THIRD FITS IN A HALLWAY.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew is gemilut chasadim, doing kindnesses, from chesed. It's the word under Micah's line, "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God": the mercy there is chesed. And the Talmud makes a surprising claim. Acts of kindness, it says, are greater than tzedakah in three ways. Tzedakah is done with money; kindness, with your body or your money. Tzedakah goes to the poor; kindness, to the poor and the rich. Tzedakah is for the living; kindness, for the living and the dead, like caring for a burial. So the pushke can't do this job for you, and nobody is too comfortable to need it. Now a neighbor who says it too. In Islam, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari to have said: every good deed is charity. In that saying, any good deed, not only money, counts as sadaqah, giving. The same instinct: the smallest kindness is on the books. And one honest difference. That saying stretches one word, charity, to cover every good deed. The Talmud keeps two words, tzedakah and chesed, and sets them side by side, each with its own job. Two maps of the same ground. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud says kindness can be done even for the rich.

segments.voice: Open your messages and choose one person who'd be glad to hear from you, someone who didn't ask. Write something small and specific: a thank-you, a memory, an offer to help with one real thing. Send it, and let that be today's kindness, done before the sit ends.

segments.voice: One kindness a day: gemilut chasadim, an act of chesed done with your hands, your time or your money, for anyone, rich or poor.
For today: chesed goes to rich and poor alike. Small enough for a hallway, and nobody has to earn it.

howItsDone: Jewish communities organize gemilut chasadim through visiting the sick, free loan societies, meals for new parents and mourners, and burial societies; individuals often make a daily small kindness part of a personal practice.
